The must-sees

  • Cathedral Square

    Square

    In 1989 the Baltic Way, a human chain of about two million people, ran from Tallinn to here. A tile marked Stebuklas, or miracle, sets the spot where it ended.

    Look for: On the square’s edge, a bronze Grand Duke Gediminas stands beside his horse, the city’s legendary founder.

  • Church of St. Peter and St. Paul

    Church

    It was built in the late 17th century for Michał Kazimierz Pac, who is buried by the entrance. A large chandelier shaped like a ship hangs in the nave.

    Look for: By the main doors, Pac’s tombstone reads “Hic iacet peccator”: here lies a sinner.

  • Gate of Dawn

    Church

    The chapel holds a painting of the Virgin Mary venerated by both Catholics and Orthodox believers. People still cross themselves or stop to pray as they pass through.

    Look for: Walk through to the outer side: above the arch, two griffins hold the Lithuanian coat of arms, the mounted knight Vytis.

  • Gediminas’ Tower

    Fortress

    It is the last standing part of the Upper Castle. In October 1988 the Lithuanian tricolour was raised here again, a step on the road to independence.

    Look for: Look east across the valley to the white Three Crosses on the neighbouring hill.

  • Hill of Three Crosses

    Viewpoint

    Concrete crosses designed by Antanas Vivulskis stood here from 1916 until the Soviet authorities blew them up in 1950. New crosses were raised in 1989, with fragments of the old ones left on the slope.

    Look for: Look west to Gediminas’ Tower on its own hill, with the cathedral and its belfry below.

  • Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights

    Museum

    The basement prison cells and execution room are preserved as they were. The names on the walls are of people killed by the Soviet security services here.

  • Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania

    Palace

    The rulers’ residence was demolished by the Russian authorities in 1801. It was rebuilt on its old foundations and opened as a museum in 2013.

    Look for: Inside, walk among the excavated foundations of the earlier palace, uncovered before the rebuilding began.

  • St. Anne’s Church

    Church

    Its front uses dozens of different brick shapes. A story says Napoleon wished he could carry it back to Paris in the palm of his hand.

    Look for: Step back to see it with the larger brick Bernardine church behind it; the two form one Gothic group.

  • Užupis District

    Neighbourhood

    On 1 April 1997 its residents declared it a tongue-in-cheek republic, with a president and an anthem. It is known for galleries, studios and riverside cafés.

    Look for: On Paupio Street, the republic’s constitution hangs on a wall in dozens of languages. One article reads: “A dog has the right to be a dog.”

  • Vilnius Cathedral

    Church

    Its present form comes from Laurynas Gucevičius in the late 18th century, on a site used for worship for centuries. The Soviets turned it into an art gallery, and it was returned to the church in 1989.

    Look for: On the roof, St Helena holds a tall cross between St Casimir and St Stanislaus. The Soviets removed the figures in 1950; today’s are replacements.

  • Vilnius University

    Culture · 1579

    Founded in 1579 by the Jesuits, it is one of the oldest universities in Central and Eastern Europe. Its Great Courtyard faces the Baroque front of St. Johns’ Church.

    Look for: In the Observatory Courtyard, find the signs of the zodiac running along the top of the old observatory building.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Vilnius and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Vilnius passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
